summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application: DAO layer (sqli/dao), views/routes, auth utilities, middlewares, app bootstrap, Jinja templates, and config. The app is riddled with classic, directly exploitable web vulnerabilities: an unauthenticated SQL injection in student creation, stored XSS enabled by globally disabled autoescaping, MD5 password hashing, CSRF protection disabled, missing authorization on every state-changing endpoint, JS-readable session cookies, and debug mode enabled. Overall risk is critical. Static assets (CSS/JS/fonts) were not reviewed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python %-formatting, splicing the attacker-controlled name directly into the SQL text instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The value flows from the POST /students/ handler (views.students, line 57: Student.create(conn, data['name'])) which reads data['name'] from the raw form with no validation and no authentication. An anonymous attacker can submit a name like `x'); DROP TABLE students; --` or use stacked queries / subqueries to read or modify arbitrary data. This is the root sink; every other DAO method in the codebase correctly uses bound parameters.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  <- name is user input from views.py:57 -> request.post()['name']. Compare to the safe Course.create which passes params to cur.execute(q, {...}).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %-formatting or f-strings.

findings.title: Stored XSS via globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled values are rendered verbatim into HTML across templates, e.g. course.jinja2 renders review.review_text, course.title and course.description, and students.jinja2 renders student name. review_text is accepted unauthenticated at POST /courses/{id}/review (views.review -> Review.create) and later rendered on the course page, giving persistent stored XSS reachable by any visitor. Combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie this allows session hijacking.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False) in app.py:33-35. Sink example course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}` with source views.py:129 Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) where review_text = data.get('review_text').
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the Jinja default) and use the |safe filter only on values known to be safe. Review each template for contexts (attributes, JS) needing additional encoding.

findings.title: Missing authorization on all state-changing endpoints
findings.description: The authorize() decorator exists but is applied only to logout (views.py:156). Every mutating handler is reachable with no authentication or role check: students (POST create), courses (POST create), review (POST create) and evaluate (POST assigns student marks). The templates hide the evaluate form behind `auth_user.is_admin`, but the handler itself performs no check, so any anonymous user can POST directly to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} to assign grades, or to /students/ and /courses/ to create records. This is a presentation-only control; server-side enforcement is absent. evaluate is shown as the representative sink because it is intended to be admin-only per course.jinja2:41.
findings.evidence: views.evaluate (lines 134-153) has no @authorize decorator; likewise views.students (51), views.courses (83), views.review (111). Only logout carries @authorize() (156). Template gate course.jinja2:41 `{% if auth_user.is_admin %}` is not mirrored server-side.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize() to all mutating handlers and @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate (and course/student creation as appropriate). Enforce authorization server-side, deny by default.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled by commenting out csrf_middleware
findings.description: The application registers session_middleware and error_middleware but the csrf_middleware line is commented out. Although templates emit a _csrf_token hidden field, no middleware validates it, so all POST endpoints (login, create student/course/review, evaluate, logout) accept cross-site forged requests. An attacker page can force an authenticated admin's browser to submit grades or create records.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[ session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware ] in app.py:25-29. csrf_middleware is fully implemented in middlewares.py:26-38 but never added to the chain.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure every state-changing form submits the token.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to md5(password). Passwords are stored as fast, unsalted MD5 digests, which are trivially brute-forced and rainbow-table reversible if the users table is leaked (e.g. via the SQL injection above). Additionally the comparison uses `==`, which is not constant-time, allowing theoretical timing analysis. MD5 is unsuitable for password storage.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  (user.py:41); import from hashlib import md5 (user.py:1).
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard password hash (Argon2id via argon2-cffi, or bcrypt) with per-user salts, and compare with the library's constant-time verify function. Rehash existing passwords on next login.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: RedisStorage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by JavaScript. Together with the stored XSS (autoescape=False), an injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie and hijack authenticated/admin sessions. No Secure flag is set either, exposing the cookie over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default), set secure=True in production, and a strict SameSite attribute.

findings.title: Debug mode enabled on the application
findings.description: The aiohttp Application is created with debug=True, enabling verbose developer behavior and more detailed error surfacing. In production this aids attackers through information disclosure and should not be hardcoded on.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production.
